chapter: Early recordings and arrival in New York
title: Claude's arrangements and unusual song forms
summary: The unusual song structures reflect Claude's influence; he hand-picked the musicians for her sessions.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: two ways. One is toward (mible) jazzing the concerts classics, which we've already discussed.
The other -- it seems to me, looking over your recording history is a relatively large number of songs which have unusual structures, but not a standard 32-bar AABA.

Right. Well this will be Claude's influence, you know, because Claude was definitely not trying to be commercial. He wasn't trying to make it simple, in other words. I mean, he really selected good music for me. And luckily enough, I could execute it, you know. Because even now, these things -- there's no way possible I could include all these in my repertoire. But there's not a one of these songs that I can't do today. And they're standards. In fact, when I travel, even as late as now, people will come up and will want to know if I still do 'Moments Like This', or do I still do 'Down the Old Ox Road', you know. These things

became identified with me.
And, of course, the arrangements were individual too. Claude took great pains to make very nice arrangements.
And it -- what actually happened, I wasn't just a singer with the band. Because a singer with the band, they get locked into the arrangements -- they do one chorus -- and then the band takes over.
But all of these were records under my own label with music accompaniments. Very good music accompaniment. And you can see the choice of musicians that he used.
I think he hand-picked these guys. It wasn't just a matter of going in and say, come on, let's make a record.
So everything worked for the best as far as I'm concerned.
